one_liner: glib-like C library whose stackful coroutine scheduler switches faster than Boost.Coroutine and libco in its author's benchmark.
what_it_does: TBOX is a large cross-platform C utility library (streams, containers, XML/JSON, networking, memory pools) with a coroutine module: stackful and stackless coroutines, a scheduler (tb_co_scheduler_init/loop), channels, semaphores, locks and coroutine-aware socket, pipe and process waits over epoll, kqueue, poll, select or IOCP. It is not a drop-in for Boost.Context or libco; you adopt tbox's own scheduler and tb_coroutine_start/tb_coroutine_yield API.
how_it_is_fast: The context switch (tb_context_jump) is a hand-written assembly routine adapted from Boost.Context's jump_fcontext: on x86-64 it pushes the six callee-saved integer registers, swaps the stack pointer and jumps, with no syscalls and no signal-mask save. tb_coroutine_yield picks the next ready coroutine and jumps to it directly, so each yield is a single coroutine-to-coroutine switch rather than a round trip through a central resumer.
when_to_use: Pure C projects that want coroutine-based network or I/O servers with built-in poller integration (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) and channels
Many-coroutine (around 1000) cooperative scheduling on one thread where switch cost dominates
Projects already using xmake or willing to take the tbox package, on x86, x86-64, ARM or ARM64
Embedded or cross-platform code that also benefits from tbox's other modules (micro build is about 64K)
when_not_to_use: You only need a context-switch primitive; minicoro, libaco or Boost.Context are far smaller dependencies than all of tbox
C++ code that wants a standard or Boost interface (C++20 coroutines, Boost.Context/Fiber); tbox's API is C and scheduler-centric
Multi-threaded work-stealing schedulers; the benchmarked scheduler runs coroutines on one thread
Code that changes the floating-point environment inside coroutines; the x86-64 jump routine does not save MXCSR or the x87 control word as Boost.Context's does
When you need a fair published comparison: the only numbers are a first-party VM benchmark from 2015-2017

integration.form: static lib (or shared lib) built with xmake; also available as an xmake package (add_requires("tbox", {configs = {coroutine = true}}))
integration.dependencies: none required for the coroutine module; optional zlib, OpenSSL/mbedTLS/PolarSSL, MySQL, SQLite3 for other modules
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (benchbox builds with c99/cxx11); xmake build system
integration.platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, BSD; coroutine switch assembly for x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the README; each scheduler and its coroutines run on the thread that loops it

gotchas: Benchmark asymmetry: in tboox/benchbox the tbox and libmill tests yield coroutine-to-coroutine through their schedulers (one jump per counted switch), while the boost (symmetric_coroutine called from main) and libco (co_resume from main, co_yield_ct back) tests bounce through main, doing two context jumps per counted switch; the reported 2.2x to 4.5x lead over boost and 3.7x to 5.7x over libco therefore overstates per-jump cost, roughly by up to 2x
libmill, measured the same scheduler-to-scheduler way, beat tbox on the LinuxMint x86-64 VM with 2 coroutines (145 ms vs 187 ms)
Debug builds enable assertions and memory checking; use the xmake release mode for performance
The x86-64 switch saves only integer callee-saved registers; floating-point control state is not preserved across switches
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tbox over libco, libgo or libfiber when you want a C coroutine runtime bundled with pollers, channels and I/O helpers in one maintained library; pick minicoro or libaco instead when you only need a tiny switch primitive, and libmill/libdill if you want a smaller C coroutine library with similar measured switch speed.
verified_claims_summary: The author's benchbox 'switch' test times 10,000,000 yields among 2 or 1000 coroutines: on a LinuxMint x86-64 VirtualBox VM tbox took 187 ms (2) and 400 ms (1000) vs Boost.Coroutine symmetric_coroutine 199/894 ms, libco 687/2288 ms and libmill 145/1014 ms; on macOS x86-64 tbox 205/438 ms vs boost 728/1949 ms. No CPU, compiler, flags or Boost version are given, and the boost and libco harnesses perform two context jumps per counted switch versus one for tbox (read from the benchbox sources).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-15, 5.1k stars, CI on Windows/Linux/macOS/Android) and Apache-2.0, but the coroutine benchmark dates from 2015-2017 and has not been rerun publicly.
